opus-5.5.text:
I think there's a lot of value there, and honestly it's one of the reasons we designed K2 the way we did. From the beginning we focused on agentic capabilities: tool use, multi-step reasoning, being able to operate over long horizons. We didn't want it to be only a chat model. So the base is meant to be something people can build on.

A general model, no matter how strong, doesn't automatically know the workflow of a specific domain. It doesn't know which tools a legal team uses, how a data analyst iterates on a problem, or what "done" means for a particular coding task. Specialized agents fill that gap. They bring the environment, the tools, the context, and sometimes the feedback signals, and the model brings the general intelligence. Together you get something much more useful than either one alone.

I also think specialization is where a lot of the real data comes from. When people build agents for concrete tasks, they discover where the model fails: where it loses track over a long trajectory, or where it calls the wrong tool. That feedback is extremely valuable for improving the next generation of models. Open-sourcing K2 is partly about this. We want many people exploring many directions in parallel, because no single team can cover every scenario.

In the long run, though, I believe the boundary will shift. Some things that need specialized engineering today will be absorbed into the base model as it gets stronger, more general, and better at learning from its environment. So I'd encourage people building on K2 to focus on what's durable: deep understanding of the task, high-quality environments, and good evaluation. Clever prompting and scaffolding to work around current weaknesses are less durable. The scaffolding may get thinner over time, but the understanding of the problem will keep its value.

So my view is that it's very valuable now, and it's also part of how the whole ecosystem, including us, gets to the next level.

r002.rationale: The response describes agent feedback as valuable for improving future models; it does not say that improvements in specialized agents are currently difficult to transfer to the base model.

fable-5.1.text:
I think specialized agents are valuable, but I'd frame it carefully, because the question of where the value sits is actually the key question for us.

Our view at Moonshot is that the base model is the thing that compounds. When we train K2, the goal is to raise the general ceiling: long-horizon reasoning, tool use, the ability to stay coherent over hundreds of steps. If the base gets those capabilities right, then building an agent for coding, or for research, or for finance becomes mostly a matter of context and tooling, not a fundamentally separate capability. So the specialized agent is a thin layer on top of something thick.

That said, I don't think "thin" means "worthless." There is real value in that layer, and it comes from a few places. One is domain knowledge that doesn't generalize well: the specific workflows, the specific tools, the taste for what a good output looks like in a particular field. Another is feedback. A specialized agent in production gives you a very concrete signal about where the model fails, and that signal flows back into training. For us that loop is probably the most important reason to build these agents at all. It's less about the product itself and more about learning what the next version of K2 needs to be.

The thing I'd warn against is over-investing in scaffolding that compensates for model weaknesses. A lot of agent engineering in the past two years was really about patching gaps: elaborate prompting, hand-written state machines, retry logic. Each new base model release erases most of that work. So if someone asks me whether they should build a specialized agent, I'd say yes, but build it in a way where the value survives when the model gets better. Put your effort into the environment, the data, the evaluation, the parts that stay useful. Don't put it into teaching the model things it will learn on its own in six months.

Longer term, I think the distinction blurs. A sufficiently capable general agent should be able to become a specialist by reading the same material a human specialist would read. We're not fully there yet, and that's exactly the gap that makes specialized agents worth building today.

astra-6.text:
I think the value is in taking a general model’s capabilities and making them useful for a specific workflow. The model is the foundation, but an agent also needs the right context, access to tools, and a way to check whether it has actually completed the task.

So building a specialized agent on K2 can be valuable when you understand a particular problem deeply: what information matters, what actions are possible, and what a good result looks like. The specialization isn’t just giving the model a different prompt. It’s building a system that can reliably do useful work in that setting.

As the underlying models improve, some of the things you previously had to engineer will become easier. But understanding users and integrating into their workflows will still matter. That’s where I would focus.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the value comes from combining a strong general model with deep knowledge of a particular workflow. K2 provides the foundation, but a specialized agent needs the right tools, context, and feedback to do useful work in a specific domain.

For example, a coding agent needs more than the ability to write code. It needs to understand the repository, run tests, interpret failures, and keep working until the task is complete. A research agent needs a different set of tools and ways to verify its results.

So the opportunity is to build that whole system around K2. The key question is whether the agent can reliably complete something valuable for the user. That’s where specialization matters.
